The vast majority of adult and fetal rhabdomyomas arise in the head and neck (e.g. in the parapharyngeal space, salivary glands, larynx, mouth, and rarely tonsil) {26246927; 24217686; 39775349; 39374098; 8319954}. Other sites include bladder {29224022}, abdomen, pelvis, extremities {24021898; 39775349}, chest, mediastinum {22520028; 11035587}, vulva {26352088}, and scrotum {23768526}.

By definition, genital rhabdomyomas arise from the genitalia, predominantly the vagina {28700439}, but paratesticular tumours are also described {23768526}.

Rhabdomyomas usually present as slow-growing, painless masses, but some grow rapidly. Multicentric tumours are associated with naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome {24517962}. Symptoms related to the local growth include proptosis, decreased vision, airway obstruction, hoarseness, obstructive sleep apnoea, hearing loss, and dysphagia {8319954}. Rare tumours are mistaken for parathyroid adenomas {30537102; 25610687}.

Adult rhabdomyomas arise as unifocal or multifocal lesions {23841004}, whereas fetal rhabdomyomas are usually solitary. Genital rhabdomyomas may present as vaginal polyps or scrotal masses.

Rhabdomyomas are distinctly rare lesions. Adult rhabdomyomas are the most common and occur in patients with a median age of 60 years (range: 33–80 years), with an M:F ratio of 3:1 {23841004}.

Fetal rhabdomyomas occur at all ages, with two peaks (< 3 years and 60 years) {26214666}. About 25% of cases are congenital {8319954}. The M:F ratio is about 1.7:1. Genital rhabdomyomas have been described in women with a mean age of 50 years and in male individuals aged 8 months to 67 years {24163862}.

Fetal rhabdomyoma may be associated with naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin syndrome), caused by loss-of-function mutations in the tumour suppressor gene PTCH1 {23780909}. Several cases have been reported with Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome {29744825}, caused by FLCN variant.

Unlike cardiac rhabdomyoma, which is considered to be a hamartoma of developing cardiac myocytes, extracardiac rhabdomyomas are considered neoplastic. PTCH1 encodes an inhibitory receptor in the sonic hedgehog signalling pathway. Inactivation of the second PTCH1 allele in syndromic fetal rhabdomyoma may fully inactivate PTCH1 function and thereby activate hedgehog signalling. Non-syndromic fetal rhabdomyomas reveal evidence of hedgehog pathway activation by an unknown mechanism {23780909}. Although adult rhabdomyomas are not associated with basal cell naevus syndrome, a few tumours show evidence of activation of the sonic hedgehog pathway {16294371}. SNP microarray has not revealed copy-number aberrations, including PTCH1 deletion or loss of heterozygosity, in genital rhabdomyoma {28700439}.

Adult rhabdomyomas form well-circumscribed, soft, nodular or lobular, deep-tan to reddish-brown masses. Tumour size ranges from 15 to 75 mm (median: 30 mm).

Fetal rhabdomyomas are well-circumscribed masses with glistening cut surfaces. Sessile or pedunculated polyps occur on mucosal surfaces. Tumour size ranges from 10 to 125 mm (median: 30 mm).

Genital rhabdomyomas in female patients form small, firm, lobulated, polypoid, non-ulcerated, epithelium-covered masses measuring 10–30 mm {8319954}. Paratesticular rhabdomyomas may partially encase the testis and spermatic cord and have a pale, glistening surface.

Rhabdomyomas form unencapsulated, lobular masses.

Adult rhabdomyomas consist of large polygonal cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, small round vesicular nuclei, and well-defined cellular borders. The cytoplasm may be vacuolated (spider cells) or may contain rod-like inclusions or cross-striations. Mitoses and clear cell change are rare {38877358}.

Classic fetal rhabdomyomas contain irregular bundles of immature skeletal muscle fibres within a myxoid background. Cells have features of fetal myotubes, i.e. spindled contours, central oblong nuclei, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. The intermediate (juvenile) subsets are more densely cellular with less myxoid stroma, and show cells with a smooth muscle phenotype and differentiated rhabdomyoblasts {8319954}. The fetal cellular subtype contains a more uniform population of differentiating myoblasts. Mitoses can be present (as many as 5 per 50 mm2). Nuclear atypia, infiltrative margins, atypical mitoses, and necrosis are absent {8319954}.

Genital rhabdomyomas in female patients are relatively small lesions (< 20 mm) that contain loose fibrous connective tissue with differentiated spindled, polygonal, or elongated rhabdomyoblasts. Many contain eosinophilic cytoplasm with cross-striations. The cells generally appear bland and lack mitoses, but some degree of cytological atypia may be present {28700439}. Vaginal lesions are polypoid but contain no cambium layer. Male genital tumours have features of adult or fetal rhabdomyomas, often with prominent sclerosis {23887159}.

Tumour cells are positive for desmin, MYOD1, and myogenin; the latter two are positive in primitive spindle cells. Desmin expression is generally strong and diffuse, and focal SMA expression may be present {23944986}.

Aspirated material shows cohesive tissue fragments of polygonal cells with round nuclei and abundant eccentric cytoplasm that may show cross-striations and intracytoplasmic vacuoles, although these are better seen in cell blocks {10740610; 21053579}.
Essential: a well-circumscribed mass with no invasion of adjacent tissues; mature rhabdomyoblasts lacking atypia and necrosis; lack of cambium layer in genital rhabdomyomas.
Complete excision of rhabdomyoma is curative, with exceptional recurrences particularly of adult rhabdomyomas after incomplete excision {19165887; 16406074}.
